questions.a: Q and S

questions.q: A craftsman melts 80 g of copper with 20 g of tin and lets the melt cool. A student examines the cooled piece, which looks like a single metal. Which description is correct?
questions.a: It is a homogeneous mixture that physical methods cannot separate into the two metals
o: It is a homogeneous mixture that physical methods cannot separate into the two metals
It is a heterogeneous mixture, because two different metals went into it
It is a solution that will separate again if the piece is left standing
It is a heterogeneous mixture whose tin can be picked out with a magnet

questions.q: Which of these mixtures, each with a gas as one component, is heterogeneous?
questions.a: fog on a winter morning
o: fog on a winter morning
soda, with carbon dioxide mixed uniformly in water
hydrogen and oxygen mixed as rocket fuel
any two gases mixed together in a closed cylinder

questions.q: Using Activity 5.1 as the model, Sara filters two tumblers through separate filter papers: tumbler A holds salt stirred into 50 mL of water and tumbler B holds chalk powder stirred into 50 mL of water. What will she find?
questions.a: A white residue stays on the paper from B, while A leaves nothing on its paper
o: A white residue stays on the paper from B, while A leaves nothing on its paper
A white residue stays on the paper from A, while B leaves nothing on its paper
Both papers keep a residue, because every mixture has two parts
Neither paper keeps a residue, because both mixtures look the same once stirred

questions.q: A sugar solution is prepared at night and kept undisturbed on a shelf for a week. Which statement is correct for the next morning?
questions.a: Spoons taken from the top and from the bottom taste equally sweet, because a solution always remains homogeneous
o: Spoons taken from the top and from the bottom taste equally sweet, because a solution always remains homogeneous
The bottom spoon is sweeter, because sugar slowly settles in every mixture
The top spoon is sweeter, because the lighter sugar rises with time
The top and bottom taste equally sweet only if the solution is stirred again before tasting

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Most mixtures of gases are homogeneous because gas particles move freely in all directions and mix uniformly.
Statement 2: Smoke is homogeneous because air, its main component, is a gas.
Statement 3: A solution, if left undisturbed for long enough, turns heterogeneous.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen used as rocket fuel is heterogeneous.
Reason (R): Gas particles move freely in all directions, so gases mix easily and uniformly.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A brass piece of 150 g is about 80% copper by mass and the rest is zinc, so it holds ___ g of zinc.

Tarun stirs one spoon of sugar into a glass of water and Neha stirs one spoon of sand into another. (a) Whose glass will taste or look the same in its first and its last sip? (b) Name the type of mixture each of them made and the observation that decides it.
questions.a: (a) Tarun's sugar glass is uniform from the first sip to the last. (b) Tarun's is a homogeneous mixture (a solution) because its composition is uniform throughout; Neha's is heterogeneous because the sand particles stay visible and settle with time.
s: (a) Identifies the sugar glass as uniform
(b) Names homogeneous and heterogeneous with the deciding observation

questions.q: A rocket fuel tank holds hydrogen and oxygen gas, while a factory chimney releases smoke into the air. (a) Which of the two is a homogeneous mixture? (b) Explain your choice in terms of how the particles are present in each.
questions.a: (a) The hydrogen and oxygen mixture is homogeneous. (b) Gas particles move freely in all directions and mix uniformly; in smoke, solid particles stay suspended in the air as a separate component, so the mixture is not uniform.
s: (a) Hydrogen and oxygen mixture identified
(b) Free-moving gas particles mix uniformly, while smoke has suspended solid particles

questions.q: Iron nails are mixed with sawdust, and separately copper is melted with zinc to make brass. Classify each result and state which one can be separated by a physical method.
questions.a: The iron nails and sawdust mixture is heterogeneous and its parts can be separated by a physical method such as a magnet; brass is a homogeneous mixture (an alloy) whose components physical methods cannot separate.
s: Classifies iron nails and sawdust as heterogeneous and brass as homogeneous
States that only the iron nails and sawdust parts separate by a physical method

questions.q: Ritu shakes cooking oil and water hard in a bottle; for a moment the bottle looks evenly cloudy. (a) What will she see after the bottle stands undisturbed? (b) Classify the mixture and justify it.
questions.a: (a) The oil and water form separate layers. (b) It is a heterogeneous mixture because the two liquids do not mix uniformly and stay as separate layers.
s: (a) Separate layers on standing
(b) Heterogeneous with the reason

questions.q: Meera says, 'If I cannot see two parts in a liquid, it must be a single substance and not a mixture.' Use a sugar solution to judge her statement.
questions.a: Her statement is not correct. A sugar solution shows no separate parts because it is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition, yet it still contains two substances, sugar and water.
s: Rejects the statement
Uses the sugar solution: uniform composition yet two substances

questions.q: True or False: Since most mixtures of gases are homogeneous, every mixture that has a gas as one of its components is homogeneous. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Smoke, fog and dust in air are heterogeneous mixtures that have a gas as one component.
s: Verdict False
Names smoke, fog or dust in air as heterogeneous with a gas component

questions.q: Imran says, 'A mixture of sand and water becomes homogeneous if I stir it hard enough.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Stirring only keeps the sand moving for a while; the sand particles remain easily visible and settle with time, so the mixture stays heterogeneous. Only a solute that dissolves, such as sugar, gives a uniform composition.
s: Verdict: not right
Sand particles stay visible and settle with time
Contrasts with a dissolved solute that gives a uniform mixture

questions.q: Write a short account of one kitchen mixture that is homogeneous and one that is heterogeneous (use examples different from sugar and sand), and for each state the observation that tells them apart.
questions.a: Example: salt in water is homogeneous; no particles are visible and every sip tastes equally salty. Example: mustard oil in water is heterogeneous; it forms separate layers or visible oil drops. Each example is paired with a uniform or non-uniform observation.
s: A valid homogeneous example with its observation
A valid heterogeneous example with its observation
Both observations point to uniform versus non-uniform composition

questions.q: A craftsman has 250 g of bronze, taken as 80% copper and 20% tin by mass. (i) Find the mass of copper and of tin in it. (ii) Say why he cannot recover the tin by filtering the bronze after crushing it, and classify bronze.
questions.a: (i) Copper = 80% of 250 g = 200 g; tin = 250 - 200 = 50 g. (ii) Bronze is an alloy, a homogeneous mixture of the metals formed by melting and mixing; physical methods cannot separate its components, so filtering does not recover the tin.
s: Copper 200 g and tin 50 g
Physical methods cannot separate an alloy
Classifies bronze as a homogeneous mixture

questions.q: Classify each of these as homogeneous or heterogeneous and give the property that decides it: (a) vinegar, (b) smoke, (c) bronze, (d) mustard oil with water, (e) soda. Then say which two of the five have a gas as a component and explain why one of them is homogeneous while the other is not.
questions.a: (a) vinegar: homogeneous, uniform throughout. (b) smoke: heterogeneous, solid particles in air. (c) bronze: homogeneous, alloy. (d) mustard oil and water: heterogeneous, separate layers. (e) soda: homogeneous, carbon dioxide mixed uniformly in water. Gas components: smoke and soda. Soda is homogeneous because the dissolved gas is mixed uniformly in the liquid; smoke is heterogeneous because its solid particles stay suspended in air as a distinct component.
s: Vinegar and soda classified homogeneous with reasons
Smoke and oil-water classified heterogeneous with reasons
Bronze classified homogeneous as an alloy
Smoke and soda identified as the gas-containing pair
Explains uniform dissolved gas versus suspended solid particles

questions.q: Three tumblers X, Y and Z each hold 100 mL of water. A student adds two spoons of sugar to X, two spoons of chalk powder to Y and a spoon of mustard oil to Z, stirs, and watches for ten minutes. (i) Describe what she will see in each tumbler at the end. (ii) Describe what the filter paper shows if X and Y are each filtered. (iii) State her conclusion about the type of mixture in each. (iv) Say which single tumbler shows the difference between the types fastest, and why.
questions.a: (i) X stays clear with nothing visible; Y shows chalk settling at the bottom; Z shows an oil layer on top of the water. (ii) X leaves nothing on the paper; Y leaves a white residue. (iii) X is homogeneous; Y and Z are heterogeneous. (iv) Z shows layers almost at once, whereas Y needs time to settle, so Z shows heterogeneity fastest.
s: Observations for all three tumblers
Filter-paper findings for X and Y
Correct classification of each
Chooses a tumbler for the fastest contrast
Reason based on layers forming at once versus settling over time

questions.q:
Pooja's lab group prepares four tumblers, each with 100 mL of water: T1 has two spoons of sugar, T2 has two spoons of fine sand, T3 has a few spoons of mustard oil and T4 has two spoons of chalk powder. After stirring well and waiting ten minutes, T1 is clear and its filter paper stays clean; sand has settled in T2; a yellow layer floats on T3; and T4 has a white powder at the bottom with its filter paper coated white.
(a) Classify each tumbler as homogeneous or heterogeneous.
(b) If T1 is left on the shelf for a whole week, what do you predict and why?
(c) A classmate says shaking T3 hard will make it homogeneous. Judge this.
(d) The teacher gives the group only one minute to show the class the contrast between the two types. Choose two tumblers to show, and state one drawback of your choice.
questions.a: (a) T1 homogeneous; T2, T3 and T4 heterogeneous. (b) T1 stays uniform throughout because a solution always remains homogeneous. (c) Shaking only mixes it for a moment; the layers re-form, so it stays heterogeneous. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. T1 with T3: the layering in T3 appears at once so it suits one minute, but T3 does not show particles settling as T2 or T4 do; T1 with T2 shows settling but needs waiting time.
s: (a) Correct classification of all four
(b) Stays homogeneous and the reason
(c) Layers re-form so the mixture is still heterogeneous
(d) Chooses two tumblers and names a drawback

questions.q:
A brass workshop in Moradabad casts a 500 g batch of brass that is about 80% copper and 20% zinc by mass. The furnace sends grey smoke into the air outside, and a worker notes that a cylinder of hydrogen and oxygen kept for another job looks like one clear gas.
(a) Find the mass of copper and of zinc in the batch.
(b) Classify brass and explain why a sieve or a magnet cannot give back its two metals.
(c) Classify the smoke and the hydrogen-oxygen mixture and say what differs in their particles.
(d) A buyer asks for a label for the batch. Choose between labelling it 'brass' and labelling it '400 g copper + 100 g zinc', and justify your choice using what the chapter says about alloys.
questions.a: (a) Copper = 400 g and zinc = 100 g. (b) Brass is a homogeneous mixture (an alloy) formed by melting and mixing; physical methods cannot separate its components. (c) Smoke is heterogeneous (solid particles suspended in air); the hydrogen-oxygen mixture is homogeneous (gas particles mix uniformly). (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. the composition label is more informative about what the material is made of, while 'brass' is simpler and brass behaves as one new material after melting.
s: (a) Copper 400 g and zinc 100 g
(b) Homogeneous alloy that physical methods cannot separate
(c) Smoke heterogeneous, hydrogen-oxygen homogeneous with the particle reason
(d) Reasoned choice of label using the chapter

questions.q: A hospital sends a 500 mL bottle of saline labelled 0.9% m/v to a ward. How much salt does the bottle contain?

Three students dissolve sugar in water: P puts 16 g in 64 g of water, Q puts 16 g in 144 g of water, R puts 28 g in 252 g of water. Which statement about their solutions is correct?
questions.a: P's solution is the most concentrated, while Q and R are equally concentrated even though R used more sugar
o: P's solution is the most concentrated, while Q and R are equally concentrated even though R used more sugar
R's solution is the most concentrated, because it contains the most sugar
P and Q are equally concentrated, because both use 16 g of sugar
All three are equally concentrated, because each is only sugar in water

questions.q: A shopkeeper in Indore wants 250 mL of vinegar that is 5% v/v acetic acid, starting from glacial acetic acid (100% acetic acid). How much glacial acetic acid must go into the final 250 mL?
o: 5 mL
50 mL

questions.q:
Match each preparation in column I with the concentration it gives in column II.
Column I: 1. 6 g of glucose dissolved in water to make 150 mL of solution  2. 9 mL of fragrance liquid mixed to make 60 mL of perfume  3. 10 g of salt dissolved in 80 g of water  4. 3.6 g of salt dissolved in water to make 400 mL of solution
Column II: a. 15%  b. 4%  c. about 11.1%  d. 0.9%

Read the statements.
Statement 1: Mass by mass percentage compares the mass of solute with the mass of the solvent alone.
Statement 2: A saline labelled 0.9% m/v has 0.9 g of salt in every 100 mL of the solution.
Statement 3: Volume by volume percentage suits mixtures of two miscible liquids, such as vinegar.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A bottle of vinegar labelled 5% v/v holds 5 mL of acetic acid in every 100 mL of the vinegar.
Reason (R): Volume by volume percentage is the method used when two miscible liquids are mixed.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: To prepare 250 g of a 12% m/m salt solution, the mass of water needed is ___ g.
(a) What does the label 0.9% m/v on a saline bottle tell you? (b) Calculate the mass of salt in a 250 mL bottle of it.
questions.a: (a) 100 mL of the solution contains 0.9 g of salt. (b) 0.9/100 x 250 = 2.25 g.
s: (a) 0.9 g of salt in 100 mL of solution

questions.q: A farmer needs a 1% v/v pesticide spray and fills a sprayer with 2 L (2000 mL) of finished spray. Calculate the volume of liquid pesticide to add and name the method of expressing concentration used.
questions.a: Volume of pesticide = 1/100 x 2000 mL = 20 mL; the method is volume by volume percentage.
s: 20 mL
Names volume by volume percentage

questions.q: A packet of spice mixture shows its salt content as a percentage. (a) Which two quantities are compared to get a percentage by mass? (b) Why does mass by mass percentage suit a dry powder when mass by volume percentage does not?
questions.a: (a) The mass of the component and the mass of the whole mixture. (b) A dry powder has no measured volume of solution, so mass by volume cannot be applied, while a mass of the whole packet can be weighed.
s: (a) Mass of component and mass of the whole mixture
(b) No volume of solution to measure in a powder, so mass is used

questions.q: A student adds 12 g of sugar to 68 g of water. (a) Find the total mass of the solution. (b) Find its mass by mass percentage.
s: (a) 80 g total

questions.q: A homemade bottle of 200 mL syrup is labelled only '5%', with no m/m, m/v or v/v. Evaluate whether the label is enough, using the amount of solute in the bottle.
questions.a: The label is not enough. If it means m/v the bottle holds 10 g of solute; if it means v/v it holds 10 mL of solute; the two are different quantities, so the method must be stated.
s: Judges the label insufficient
Shows 10 g versus 10 mL for the same 5%

questions.q: True or False: A solution made by dissolving 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water is 20% m/m. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The mass of the solution is 20 + 100 = 120 g, so the mass by mass percentage is 20/120 x 100, about 16.7%.
s: Verdict False
Corrects the denominator to the total mass 120 g, giving about 16.7%

questions.q: Deepa says, 'A saline labelled 0.9% m/v means 0.9 g of salt is dissolved in 100 mL of water.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The amount, 0.9 g of salt per 100 mL, is correct, but the 100 mL is the volume of the whole solution, not of the water added.
s: Verdict: partly right
0.9 g of salt per 100 mL is correct
The 100 mL is of the solution, not the water

questions.q: A student reports that her salt solution is 120% m/m. Show that this result cannot be correct.
questions.a: Mass by mass percentage is solute mass divided by the mass of the solution, times 100. The solution contains the solute plus the solvent, so the solute mass is always less than the solution mass and the value cannot reach 100%, let alone 120%.
s: States the formula with the mass of the solution in the denominator
Solution mass = solute + solvent, so it is larger than the solute mass
Concludes the percentage is below 100 so 120% is impossible

questions.q: Three tablespoons of 15 mL orange squash concentrate are mixed with water to make 180 mL of juice. Calculate the % v/v of the concentrate and explain why this is the method to use.
questions.a: Volume of concentrate = 3 x 15 = 45 mL; % v/v = 45/180 x 100 = 25%. The method is suitable because both the concentrate and the juice are liquids measured by volume.
s: 45 mL of concentrate
Reason: liquids measured by volume, so volume by volume percentage

questions.q: Three preparations are made: (i) 8 g of salt in 72 g of water, (ii) 8 g of glucose dissolved in water to make 160 mL of solution, (iii) 8 mL of a fragrance liquid mixed to make 40 mL of perfume. Calculate each concentration with the proper method, and explain why the answers for (i) and (ii) cannot be compared directly.
questions.a: (i) 8/80 x 100 = 10% m/m. (ii) 8/160 x 100 = 5% m/v. (iii) 8/40 x 100 = 20% v/v. The first is grams per 100 g of solution and the second is grams per 100 mL of solution, so they use different denominators and units and describe different things.
s: (i) 10% m/m with total mass 80 g
(ii) 5% m/v
(iii) 20% v/v
Names the method for each
Explains different denominators and units block a direct comparison

questions.q: Three students make sugar solutions: Anu dissolves 24 g of sugar in 96 g of water, Bela dissolves 24 g in 120 g of water, and Charu dissolves 36 g in 144 g of water. (i) Find the % m/m of each. (ii) Who has the most concentrated solution, and is it the one with most sugar? (iii) Anu adds 10 g more water to her solution; find its new % m/m and say what that does to its concentration.
questions.a: (i) Anu: 24/120 x 100 = 20%. Bela: 24/144 x 100 = about 16.7%. Charu: 36/180 x 100 = 20%. (ii) Anu and Charu are equally the most concentrated at 20%, though Charu used more sugar; concentration depends on the ratio, not on the amount of sugar alone. (iii) New total = 130 g, so 24/130 x 100 = about 18.5%; adding water lowers the concentration.
s: Anu and Bela calculated
Charu calculated
Identifies the tie and that more sugar does not mean more concentrated
New percentage about 18.5%
States that adding solvent lowers the concentration

questions.q:
The pharmacy of a district hospital in Nagpur has to prepare 2 L (2000 mL) of 0.9% m/v saline and 500 mL of 5% m/v glucose solution for the evening. The store holds 25 g of salt and only 20 g of glucose.
(a) Calculate the mass of salt needed for the saline.
(b) Calculate the mass of glucose needed and say whether the stock is enough.
(c) Why do hospitals state such drips in mass by volume percentage rather than mass by mass?
(d) The pharmacist can either make the full 500 mL using all 20 g of glucose, or make a smaller batch of the correct strength. Choose one and justify it with the chapter's idea of proportion.
questions.a: (a) 0.9/100 x 2000 = 18 g. (b) 5/100 x 500 = 25 g, so the 20 g of glucose is not enough. (c) In medicines it is easier to measure a volume of liquid than to weigh it. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. making 400 mL at the correct 5% m/v (20 g in 400 mL) because the right proportion is essential, at the cost of a smaller volume; the 500 mL option would be only 4% m/v.
s: (a) 18 g of salt
(b) 25 g needed and the stock is short
(c) Volume is easier to measure than weighing a liquid
(d) A justified choice with the 400 mL or 4% figures

questions.q:
Gopal, a farmer in Nashik, must spray his rice crop with a 1% v/v pesticide solution. His sprayer tank takes 15 L (15000 mL) of finished spray, but he has only a 120 mL bottle of the liquid pesticide left. The chapter notes that too little pesticide may not protect the crop, while too much can damage crops, soil and the environment.
(a) How much pesticide does one full 15 L tank need?
(b) If he pours his 120 mL into one full 15 L tank, what is the % v/v of the spray?
(c) What is likely to happen at that strength, according to the chapter?
(d) Gopal can either spray the weaker 15 L tank now or make a smaller correct-strength batch and spray less area. Choose one and justify it.
questions.a: (a) 1/100 x 15000 = 150 mL. (b) 120/15000 x 100 = 0.8% v/v. (c) Too little pesticide may not protect the crop. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. a 12 L batch (120 mL in 12000 mL gives 1%) keeps the proper strength but covers less area; the weaker 15 L tank covers more area but risks poor protection.
s: (c) Too little may not protect the crop
(d) A reasoned choice naming the trade-off

questions.q: Two identical bottles of a fizzy drink are opened at the same time: one stays in a refrigerator and the other is left in warm sunshine. Which bottle loses its fizz faster, and why?
questions.a: The warm one, because the solubility of a gas in a liquid generally decreases as temperature rises
o: The warm one, because the solubility of a gas in a liquid generally decreases as temperature rises

questions.q: At 40 degrees Celsius, 40 g of potassium nitrate is stirred into 50 g of water (solubility 62 g per 100 g of water at that temperature). What is the result?
questions.a: A saturated solution forms and 9 g of the salt stays undissolved
o: A saturated solution forms and 9 g of the salt stays undissolved
An unsaturated solution forms because all 40 g dissolves
A saturated solution forms and 31 g of the salt stays undissolved
A saturated solution forms and all 40 g dissolves, then settles on cooling

questions.q: Two equal portions of the same hot saturated copper sulfate solution are kept apart: one is cooled quickly in ice-cold water and the other is left to cool slowly at room temperature without being disturbed. What is expected?
questions.a: The quickly cooled portion gives smaller, less well-formed crystals than the slowly cooled one
o: The quickly cooled portion gives smaller, less well-formed crystals than the slowly cooled one
The quickly cooled portion gives larger, better-shaped crystals than the slowly cooled one
Both portions give crystals of exactly the same size and shape
Only the slowly cooled portion gives crystals; the other stays a clear liquid

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Solubility is stated for a fixed quantity of solvent, such as 100 g, at a given temperature.
Statement 2: The solubility of a gas dissolved in a liquid generally increases as temperature increases.
Statement 3: Crystallization of a substance from solution rests on its different solubility at different temperatures.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cooling a saturated solution of potassium nitrate from 60 degrees Celsius to 20 degrees Celsius makes crystals appear.
Reason (R): The solubility of potassium nitrate is lower at 20 degrees Celsius than at 60 degrees Celsius, so the excess solute separates out.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate made with 100 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius is cooled to 40 degrees Celsius; using Table 5.4, ___ g of solid separates out.

(a) Using Table 5.4, what mass of potassium nitrate is needed to saturate 250 g of water at 40 degrees Celsius? (b) A student adds only 140 g to that water. Is the solution saturated, and how much more can dissolve?
questions.a: (a) 62/100 x 250 = 155 g. (b) No; it is not saturated, and 155 - 140 = 15 g more can dissolve.
s: (b) Unsaturated, 15 g more

questions.q: A saturated solution of potassium chloride in 100 g of water at 60 degrees Celsius is cooled to 10 degrees Celsius. Using Table 5.4, predict what is observed and how much solid appears.
questions.a: Solid crystals separate out as the solution cools because solubility falls from 46 g to 35 g per 100 g of water; the amount is 46 - 35 = 11 g.
s: Observation: solid separates on cooling, with the reason
Amount: 11 g

questions.q: (a) Why must the temperature be mentioned whenever the solubility of a substance is stated? (b) State in which direction the solubility changes with a rise in temperature for a solid in a liquid and for a gas in a liquid.
questions.a: (a) Because the solubility of a substance changes with temperature. (b) For a solid in a liquid it generally increases; for a gas in a liquid it generally decreases.
s: (a) Solubility depends on temperature
(b) Solid increases, gas decreases

questions.q: Using Table 5.4, compare the rise in solubility of potassium nitrate and of potassium chloride between 20 and 60 degrees Celsius, and say which would deposit more solid when a hot saturated solution is cooled from 60 to 20 degrees Celsius.
questions.a: Potassium nitrate rises from 32 to 106, a rise of 74 g per 100 g of water; potassium chloride rises from 35 to 46, a rise of 11 g. Potassium nitrate would deposit more solid, since its solubility changes much more.
s: Rises of 74 g and 11 g calculated
Potassium nitrate deposits more, because it changes more

questions.q: A student wants to obtain sodium chloride crystals by dissolving it to saturation in hot water at 80 degrees Celsius and then cooling the solution to 10 degrees Celsius. Using Table 5.4, evaluate her plan.
questions.a: The plan is poor. Sodium chloride has a solubility of 37 g per 100 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius and 36 g at 10 degrees Celsius, so only about 1 g per 100 g of water would separate.
s: Judges the plan poor
Uses 37 g versus 36 g, about 1 g deposited

questions.q: True or False: A solution of a solid that is saturated at 40 degrees Celsius can usually dissolve more of the solid if it is heated. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The solubility of a solid in a liquid generally increases with temperature, so the warmer solution can hold more solute.
s: Verdict True
Solubility of a solid in a liquid generally rises with temperature

questions.q: Farida says, 'Warming a bottle of soda lets the liquid hold more dissolved gas, because solubility always increases with temperature.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The solubility of a solid in a liquid generally increases with temperature, but that of a gas dissolved in a liquid generally decreases, so warming the soda lets the gas escape.
s: Verdict: not right
Solid solubility generally increases with temperature
Gas solubility generally decreases, so soda loses gas when warmed

questions.q: Write two made-up rows for a solubility table (values at 10 and 80 degrees Celsius, in g per 100 g of water): one salt that is well suited to purification by cooling a hot saturated solution and one that is not. Give a reason for each.
questions.a: Example: salt P, 20 g at 10 degrees Celsius and 160 g at 80 degrees Celsius, is suitable because cooling deposits about 140 g per 100 g of water. Salt Q, 35 g at 10 degrees Celsius and 36 g at 80 degrees Celsius, is not suitable because cooling deposits only about 1 g.
s: A row with a large rise in solubility
A row with a very small rise
A reason for each based on the amount that separates on cooling

questions.q: A saturated solution of potassium nitrate is made with 150 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius and cooled to 20 degrees Celsius. Using Table 5.4, find the mass dissolved at each temperature and the mass of crystals formed.
questions.a: At 80 degrees Celsius: 167 x 1.5 = 250.5 g dissolved. At 20 degrees Celsius: 32 x 1.5 = 48 g can stay dissolved. Crystals formed = 250.5 - 48 = 202.5 g.
s: 250.5 g at 80 degrees Celsius
48 g at 20 degrees Celsius
202.5 g of crystals

questions.q: Using Table 5.4, work out the change in solubility of potassium nitrate, sodium chloride, potassium chloride and ammonium chloride between 10 and 80 degrees Celsius. Arrange the four in order of the change, state the general effect of temperature on these salts, and say which of the four would be easiest and which hardest to purify by crystallization.
questions.a: Changes per 100 g of water: potassium nitrate 167 - 21 = 146 g; ammonium chloride 66 - 24 = 42 g; potassium chloride 54 - 35 = 19 g; sodium chloride 37 - 36 = 1 g. Order: potassium nitrate > ammonium chloride > potassium chloride > sodium chloride. In general solubility increases with temperature. Potassium nitrate is easiest, sodium chloride is hardest.
s: All four changes calculated
Correct order of the four
General effect: solubility increases with temperature
Easiest and hardest named with reason

questions.q: Think as a Scientist: the hypothesis is that a hot saturated copper sulfate solution cooled rapidly forms smaller, less well-formed crystals than one cooled slowly. Plan an experiment: (i) say how the solution is divided and what is cooled how; (ii) name two things that must be kept the same; (iii) say what is observed or compared; (iv) state the result that supports the hypothesis; (v) name one safety precaution.
questions.a: (i) Prepare a hot saturated solution and divide it into two equal parts; cool one rapidly in ice-cold water and the other slowly at room temperature without disturbing it. (ii) Keep the same volume and concentration of the solution, and the same starting temperature. (iii) Compare the size and shape of the crystals after filtering and drying. (iv) Smaller, less well-formed crystals in the rapidly cooled part support it. (v) Copper sulfate is toxic: work under adult supervision and do not touch it with bare hands.
s: Division into two equal parts and the two cooling conditions
Two controlled variables
What is compared
Result that supports the hypothesis
A safety precaution

questions.q:
A school laboratory in Pune prepares potassium nitrate crystals. The class makes a saturated solution with 300 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius and then cools it. Table 5.4 gives the solubility of potassium nitrate per 100 g of water: 21 g at 10 degrees Celsius, 62 g at 40 degrees Celsius, 32 g at 20 degrees Celsius and 167 g at 80 degrees Celsius.
(a) How much potassium nitrate dissolves in the 300 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius?
(b) How much solid separates when the solution is cooled to 20 degrees Celsius?
(c) Why does the solid separate at all?
(d) The teacher offers two options: cool only to 40 degrees Celsius using tap water, or cool to 10 degrees Celsius using ice. Choose one, giving the mass of crystals expected for each.
questions.a: (a) 167 x 3 = 501 g. (b) 501 - 96 = 405 g. (c) Solubility falls as temperature drops, so the extra solute cannot stay dissolved. (d) Cooling to 40 degrees Celsius gives 501 - 186 = 315 g; cooling to 10 degrees Celsius gives 501 - 63 = 438 g; a reasoned choice: ice gives 123 g more but needs more effort, while tap water is simpler but gives less.
s: (c) Solubility decreases on cooling
(d) A justified choice using 315 g and 438 g

questions.q:
A student mixes 30 g of potassium nitrate with 2 g of sodium chloride and dissolves both completely in 50 g of water at 80 degrees Celsius. She then cools the solution slowly. Assume that each salt dissolves independently of the other and use Table 5.4: potassium nitrate has solubility 167, 32 and 21 g per 100 g of water at 80, 20 and 10 degrees Celsius; sodium chloride has 37 and 36 g at 80 and 10 degrees Celsius.
(a) Show that both salts dissolve fully at 80 degrees Celsius in 50 g of water.
(b) How much potassium nitrate separates on cooling to 20 degrees Celsius?
(c) Does the sodium chloride crystallize at 10 degrees Celsius? Explain.
(d) She needs at least 17 g of potassium nitrate crystals from this batch. Decide whether cooling to 20 degrees Celsius is enough or 10 degrees Celsius is needed, and justify with a calculation.
questions.a: (a) 50 g of water can hold 83.5 g of potassium nitrate and 18.5 g of sodium chloride at 80 degrees Celsius, both more than the amounts used. (b) At 20 degrees Celsius 50 g of water holds 16 g, so 30 - 16 = 14 g separates. (c) No; at 10 degrees Celsius 50 g of water can hold 18 g of sodium chloride, more than 2 g, so it stays dissolved. (d) At 20 degrees Celsius 50 g of water holds 16 g, so 14 g separates, less than 17 g; at 10 degrees Celsius it holds 10.5 g, so 30 - 10.5 = 19.5 g separates, more than 17 g. Cool to 10 degrees Celsius; the 2 g of sodium chloride still stays dissolved.
s: (a) Capacity 83.5 g and 18.5 g exceed the amounts
(b) 14 g of potassium nitrate
(c) No, it stays dissolved
(d) 14 g is below 17 g, 19.5 g is above it, so 10 degrees Celsius

questions.q: A technician reads Table 5.5 (alcohol boils at 78 degrees Celsius, benzene at 80 degrees Celsius) and says, 'Ordinary distillation will do, since the two boil at different temperatures.' What should he be told?
questions.a: Use fractional distillation, because they differ by only 2 degrees Celsius, far below the limit of about 25 degrees Celsius
o: Use fractional distillation, because they differ by only 2 degrees Celsius, far below the limit of about 25 degrees Celsius
Use ordinary distillation, because any difference at all in boiling points is enough
Use evaporation, because acetone and benzene are solids
Use ordinary distillation, because any two liquids can be separated if one boils lower

questions.q: A student heats a mixture of acetone and water in a distillation flask and passes the vapour through a water-cooled condenser into a conical flask. What does she collect first, and what stays behind in the distillation flask?
questions.a: Acetone is collected as the distillate, while water stays behind in the flask
o: Acetone is collected as the distillate, while water stays behind in the flask
Water is collected as the distillate, while acetone stays behind in the flask
Acetone and water are collected together, with nothing left in the flask
Acetone stays behind, because the condenser removes the water first

questions.q: Salt water is heated in a distillation flask and the vapour is condensed in a separate vessel. What is found in the vessel and in the flask at the end?
questions.a: Pure water in the vessel and the salt left in the flask
o: Pure water in the vessel and the salt left in the flask
Salt water in the vessel and pure salt in the flask
Pure water in the vessel and no residue in the flask
Salt in the vessel and pure water left in the flask

questions.q: Which set-up is correct for paper chromatography of a black sketch-pen spot?
questions.a: A pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the strip, the ink spot on it, and the lower end dipping into a thin layer of water that stays below the spot
o: A pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the strip, the ink spot on it, and the lower end dipping into a thin layer of water that stays below the spot
The ink spot placed at the very bottom edge of the strip, which is dipped fully into deep water
The line drawn with the same black sketch pen, with the water level kept above the line
The strip laid flat on a dry table with a drop of water placed on the ink spot

questions.q:
Match each separation task in column I with the method in column II.
Column I: 1. Acetone (boils at 56 degrees Celsius) from water (100 degrees Celsius)  2. Alcohol (78 degrees Celsius) from benzene (80 degrees Celsius)  3. The coloured pigments in a green leaf extract  4. Pure crystals of a salt whose solubility rises steeply with temperature, from its hot saturated solution
Column II: a. Paper chromatography  b. Fractional distillation  c. Distillation  d. Crystallization

Read the statements.
Statement 1: Distillation can give back the liquid from a solution that has a solid dissolved in it.
Statement 2: Fractional distillation is used for liquids whose boiling points differ by less than about 25 degrees Celsius.
Statement 3: In paper chromatography, components are separated by how fast the liquid carries them up the paper.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Acetone can be separated from water by distillation.
Reason (R): Acetone and water have the same boiling point.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Liquid P boils at 56 degrees Celsius and liquid Q boils 22 degrees Celsius above it, so Q boils at ___ degrees Celsius.

(a) Using Table 5.5, find the difference between the boiling points of water (100 degrees Celsius) and alcohol (78 degrees Celsius). (b) Say whether simple distillation or fractional distillation suits their mixture.
questions.a: (a) 100 - 78 = 22 degrees Celsius. (b) Fractional distillation, because the difference is less than about 25 degrees Celsius.
s: (a) 22 degrees Celsius
(b) Fractional distillation with the reason

questions.q: In the distillation of an acetone and water mixture, (a) what happens to the vapour in the condenser, and (b) why does the water stay in the distillation flask?
questions.a: (a) The vapour of acetone is cooled by circulating water or air and condenses back into pure liquid. (b) Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, much higher than acetone, so its vapours are not formed in significant amounts while acetone is being collected.
s: (a) Cooled by circulating water or air and condensed
(b) Water's much higher boiling point

questions.q: A drop of water spreads a black sketch-pen spot on a paper strip into three coloured spots at different heights. (a) What does this show about the ink? (b) What decides how far each colour travels?
questions.a: (a) The black ink is a mixture of at least three coloured components. (b) How fast each component is carried by the liquid, which depends on its interactions with the solvent and the paper.
s: (a) The ink is a mixture of components
(b) Speed set by interaction with the solvent and the paper

questions.q: Rani tries to separate the pigments in a spinach leaf extract using water as the solvent, but the colours hardly move. She concludes that paper chromatography cannot separate them. Evaluate her conclusion.
questions.a: Her conclusion is not justified. Water does not work as the solvent in every case; a different solvent such as alcohol, or a mixture of solvents, may be needed.
s: Rejects the conclusion
Suggests another solvent such as alcohol or a solvent mixture

questions.q: Why can distillation give both liquids of an acetone and water mixture, while simply evaporating the mixture cannot?
questions.a: In evaporation the liquid that turns to vapour escapes into the air and is lost. In distillation the vapour is passed through a condenser and cooled back to liquid, so it is collected separately and the other liquid remains behind.
s: Evaporation loses the vapour
Distillation condenses and collects it

questions.q: True or False: Evaporating a salt solution to dryness gives the salt but loses the water, whereas distillation can recover the water as well. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. In evaporation the solvent disappears into the air, while in distillation its vapour is condensed and collected, leaving the dissolved solid in the flask.
s: Verdict True
Solvent is lost by evaporation but condensed and collected by distillation

questions.q: Dev says, 'When I distil a mixture of water and acetone, the first liquid that condenses and drips into the receiver will be acetone.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Acetone boils at about 56 degrees Celsius and water at 100 degrees Celsius, so the lower-boiling acetone vaporises first and is condensed and collected, while the water stays in the flask.
s: Verdict: right
Acetone has the lower boiling point, 56 against 100 degrees Celsius
Lower-boiling liquid vaporises, condenses and is collected first

questions.q: Show that a mixture of alcohol (78 degrees Celsius) and benzene (80 degrees Celsius) cannot be separated well by simple distillation.
questions.a: The boiling points differ by only 80 - 78 = 2 degrees Celsius, far below the difference of about 25 degrees Celsius needed. Both liquids would form significant vapour together, so the distillate would be a mixture; fractional distillation is needed.
s: Difference of 2 degrees Celsius calculated
Compared with the 25 degrees Celsius requirement
Both vaporise together so a clean separation fails; fractional distillation needed

questions.q: Using Table 5.5, decide the method for each miscible pair and give the boiling-point difference: (i) acetone and alcohol, (ii) alcohol and chloroform, (iii) water and acetone.
questions.a: (i) 78 - 56 = 22 degrees Celsius, fractional distillation. (ii) 78 - 61 = 17 degrees Celsius, fractional distillation. (iii) 100 - 56 = 44 degrees Celsius, simple distillation.
s: Differences 22, 17 and 44 degrees Celsius
Fractional distillation for the first two
Simple distillation for water and acetone

questions.q: Choose the best method for each task and give a reason: (i) pure acetone from an acetone and water mixture; (ii) pure crystals of potassium nitrate from its hot saturated solution; (iii) drinking water from salty water when the water is wanted; (iv) the salt from salt solution when the water is not wanted; (v) the separate colours in a black ink.
questions.a: (i) Distillation, as the boiling points differ by 44 degrees Celsius. (ii) Crystallization, because its solubility falls on cooling. (iii) Distillation, because the water vapour can be condensed and collected. (iv) Evaporation of the water, which leaves the salt. (v) Paper chromatography, because the colours move at different speeds.
s: (i) Distillation with the boiling-point reason
(ii) Crystallization with the solubility reason
(iii) Distillation so the water is recovered
(iv) Evaporation to leave the salt
(v) Paper chromatography with the speed reason

questions.q: Rina has a green food colour and a fresh spinach leaf extract and wants to see how many pigments each contains. Plan the paper chromatography: (i) how to prepare each strip; (ii) how deep the liquid should be and where it stands relative to the spot; (iii) what she should see as the liquid rises if the colour is a mixture; (iv) what she can do if the spinach pigments hardly move in water; (v) what she can compare at the end.
questions.a: (i) Cut a strip of chromatographic paper, draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom and put a spot of the sample on it. (ii) Use only a thin layer of liquid so the level stays below the spot. (iii) The colour separates into different coloured spots as the liquid carries the components up at different speeds. (iv) Try another solvent such as alcohol or a mixture of solvents. (v) The number of spots and how far each travelled for the two samples.
s: Strip prepared with pencil line and spot
Thin layer of liquid below the spot
Separate coloured spots as components move at different speeds
Another solvent such as alcohol if water fails
Comparison of spots between samples

questions.q:
A student at a school in Hyderabad distils 100 mL of an acetone and water mixture and notes the thermometer at the neck of the distillation flask. Her record: from 0 to 10 minutes the reading climbs to 56 degrees Celsius; from 10 to 25 minutes it stays near 56 degrees Celsius while clear liquid drips into the conical flask; after 25 minutes the reading climbs past 90 degrees Celsius and the dripping almost stops.
(a) What was collected between 10 and 25 minutes?
(b) Why does the reading rise after 25 minutes?
(c) Calculate the boiling-point difference of the two liquids and say whether simple distillation was suitable.
(d) She can stop at 25 minutes to keep the liquid purer, or carry on to get a little more liquid. Choose one and say what is risked.
questions.a: (a) Acetone, as the lower-boiling liquid, condensed and collected. (b) Most of the acetone has gone and the remaining liquid is mainly water, which boils at 100 degrees Celsius. (c) 100 - 56 = 44 degrees Celsius, which is more than 25, so simple distillation was suitable. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. stopping at 25 minutes keeps the acetone pure but leaves some behind; carrying on gains a little more liquid but risks collecting water vapour with it.
s: (a) Acetone collected
(b) The remaining liquid is mainly water boiling at 100 degrees Celsius
(c) 44 degrees Celsius and simple distillation suitable
(d) A reasoned choice naming the risk

questions.q:
A school inquiry compares three black inks by paper chromatography under identical conditions (the same paper, the same solvent and the same time). The ink from a note separates into spots at 2.0 cm, 3.5 cm and 5.0 cm above the start line. Pen X gives spots at 2.0, 3.5 and 5.0 cm. Pen Y gives two spots at 2.0 and 4.0 cm. Pen Z gives four spots at 2.0, 3.5, 5.0 and 6.5 cm.
(a) How many components does the note's ink have?
(b) Which pen's ink matches the note, and why?
(c) Why do the spots stop at different heights?
(d) Decide whether pen Z can have written the note, and whether pen X can be named with certainty. Justify both.
questions.a: (a) Three components. (b) Pen X, because its spots appear at the same three heights as the note's. (c) Each component moves at a different speed, set by its interaction with the solvent and the paper. (d) Pen Z cannot have written the note: it has a fourth component (6.5 cm) that the note's ink lacks. Pen X matches all three spots, so it is consistent with the note, but another pen with the same ink would give the same spots, so X cannot be named with certainty.
s: (a) Three components
(b) Pen X with the matching spot heights
(c) Different speeds from interactions with solvent and paper
(d) Rules out Z (extra spot) and keeps X only as consistent

questions.q: A student pours 5 mL of mustard oil and 20 mL of water into a separating funnel and lets it stand. Which procedure gives two separate liquids?
questions.a: Drain the lower water layer slowly, close the stopcock as the water is almost gone, discard the small mixed portion, then collect the oil
o: Drain the lower water layer slowly, close the stopcock as the water is almost gone, discard the small mixed portion, then collect the oil
Drain the upper oil layer first through the stopcock, then drain the water
Open the stopcock fully so that both liquids run out together into one container
Drain the water, close the stopcock, and then collect the mixed portion along with the oil

questions.q: A shopkeeper knows that 1 L of cooking oil has a mass of 910 g and 1 L of water has a mass of 1000 g. When a little oil spills into a bucket of water, what is seen?
questions.a: The oil forms a layer on top of the water, because for the same volume the oil has less mass
o: The oil forms a layer on top of the water, because for the same volume the oil has less mass
The oil sinks below the water, because oil is thicker than water
The oil dissolves completely in the water to give a uniform liquid
The oil forms a layer on top, because for the same volume the oil has more mass

questions.q: A student heats a mixture of crushed naphthalene and sand in a china dish and covers it with an inverted funnel plugged with cotton. What is seen after a few minutes?
questions.a: Solid deposits form on the inner wall of the funnel, while the sand stays in the dish
o: Solid deposits form on the inner wall of the funnel, while the sand stays in the dish
Liquid naphthalene collects in the dish while the sand sinks through it
Sand deposits on the funnel wall, while the naphthalene stays in the dish
Nothing deposits on the funnel because naphthalene cannot leave the dish

questions.q: An ice-cream vendor packs dry ice around the tubs. After some hours the dry ice has vanished and there is no puddle in the box. What explains this?
questions.a: Solid carbon dioxide sublimes, changing directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state
o: Solid carbon dioxide sublimes, changing directly into vapour without passing through the liquid state
The dry ice melts first and the liquid carbon dioxide then dissolves in the ice cream
The dry ice undergoes deposition, changing from vapour to a solid in the air
The dry ice dissolves in the water of the ice cream, leaving no solid behind

questions.q: While draining water from a separating funnel, a student forgets to close the stopcock and lets the oil begin to flow into the same container. What goes wrong?
questions.a: A portion that contains both liquids is collected with the water, so the water is no longer pure
o: A portion that contains both liquids is collected with the water, so the water is no longer pure
Only the oil is affected, because the water has already been collected completely
The oil layer is lost, because oil cannot pass through the stopcock
Nothing goes wrong, because immiscible liquids cannot mix while draining

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: In a separating funnel the denser of two immiscible liquids forms the upper layer.
Statement 2: Camphor, on heating below its melting point, changes directly from solid to vapour.
Statement 3: Deposition is the change of a solid directly into vapour on heating.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 only
3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When mustard oil and water are poured into a separating funnel, the oil forms the upper layer.
Reason (R): Mustard oil and water are immiscible liquids.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: If cooking oil has a mass of 910 g per litre, a 2.5 L can of it holds ___ g of oil.
(a) In a separating funnel holding mustard oil and water, which liquid forms the upper layer and what property decides it? (b) Which liquid leaves first through the stopcock?
questions.a: (a) Mustard oil forms the upper layer because it is less dense than water. (b) The denser lower layer, water, is drained first.
s: (a) Oil on top because it is less dense
(b) Water drains first

questions.q: Why does the student close the stopcock when the water is almost fully drained, and what is done with the next small portion that flows out?
questions.a: The stopcock is closed so that the mixed region between the layers is not collected with the water. The small portion that may contain both liquids is collected separately and discarded, and then the oil is collected.
s: Closes the stopcock to avoid collecting the mixed portion
The mixed portion is discarded before the oil is collected

questions.q: A mixture of camphor and sand is heated gently in a china dish. (a) What happens to each substance? (b) Name the change by which camphor leaves the dish and the change by which it forms deposits on the funnel.
questions.a: (a) The camphor changes to vapour and leaves the dish while the sand stays unchanged. (b) Sublimation takes the camphor away and deposition forms the solid on the cooler funnel wall.
s: (a) Camphor vaporises, sand stays
(b) Sublimation and deposition named

questions.q: A drum receives 3 L of cooking oil (910 g per litre) and 3 L of water (1000 g per litre). Find the mass of each liquid and say which one forms the top layer.
questions.a: Oil: 3 x 910 = 2730 g. Water: 3 x 1000 = 3000 g. The oil has less mass for the same volume, so it forms the top layer.
s: 2730 g of oil and 3000 g of water
Oil is on top because it is less dense

questions.q: Meena says, 'Sublimation is the same as evaporation, only faster.' Judge her statement.
questions.a: Her statement is not correct. In evaporation a liquid changes to vapour, whereas in sublimation a solid changes directly into vapour on heating without passing through the liquid state.
s: Rejects the statement
Distinguishes liquid to vapour from solid to vapour without a liquid state

questions.q: True or False: When a mixture of camphor and sand is heated, the camphor first melts into a liquid and is then poured off from the sand. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Camphor, heated below its melting point, changes directly from solid to vapour without a liquid state, and the vapour deposits as a solid on the cooler funnel.
s: Verdict False
Corrects it: direct solid to vapour change, then deposition on the funnel

questions.q: Hema separates oil from water with a separating funnel and says, 'The oil is on top, so I should collect the oil first through the stopcock.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The stopcock is at the bottom, so the lower, denser water layer drains first. The stopcock is closed when the water is almost gone, the mixed portion is discarded, and only then is the oil collected.
s: Verdict: not right
The lower layer reaches the stopcock first
Correct order: water, discard the mixed portion, then oil

questions.q: Show that the camphor-and-sand method cannot separate a mixture of camphor and naphthalene.
questions.a: The method works because one solid sublimes and the other, sand, does not. Camphor and naphthalene both sublime on heating, so both would turn to vapour and deposit on the funnel together, and no separation is achieved.
s: States that the method needs one sublimable and one non-sublimable solid
Both camphor and naphthalene sublime
Both deposit together so no separation results

questions.q: A 5 L can of cooking oil is labelled 4.55 kg. If it is poured into a tank of water (1 L of water has a mass of 1000 g), will it form a separate layer, which liquid is on top, and how can the two be separated?
questions.a: The oil has 4550 g / 5 L = 910 g per litre, less than the 1000 g per litre of water. It does not mix, so it forms a separate layer on top of the water, and a separating funnel is used to separate them.
s: 910 g per litre calculated
Forms a layer with oil on top, because it is less dense
Separating funnel named for the separation

questions.q: A mixture contains sand, common salt and naphthalene. Plan a sequence of separation steps to get all three, saying which technique is used at each stage and why that stage comes where it does.
questions.a: Step 1: heat the mixture gently so naphthalene sublimes and collects as a solid on a cool funnel; this comes first because only naphthalene sublimes. Step 2: add water to the remaining sand and salt; the salt dissolves and the sand does not. Step 3: filter, so the sand stays on the filter paper. Step 4: evaporate the water from the filtrate, or crystallize it, to get the salt.
s: Sublimation of naphthalene first, with the reason
Adding water so the salt dissolves and the sand does not
Filtration leaves the sand
Evaporation or crystallization of the filtrate gives the salt
Order justified: each method uses a different property

questions.q: Write a numbered procedure for separating 8 mL of mustard oil from 32 mL of water using a 50 mL separating funnel. For each of the main stages say what the student does and what is seen or collected, and give the volume of the liquid in the funnel at the start.
questions.a: The volume is 8 + 32 = 40 mL, within the 50 mL funnel. (1) Pour the mixture in and let it stand. (2) Two layers form, yellow oil above and water below. (3) Open the stopcock slowly and collect the water in a container. (4) Close the stopcock when the water is almost fully drained. (5) Collect and discard the small mixed portion. (6) Open the stopcock again and collect the oil separately.
s: Total volume 40 mL checked against the 50 mL funnel
Standing and layers: oil above, water below
Draining the lower water layer slowly
Closing near the end and discarding the mixed portion
Collecting the oil separately

questions.q:
A camphor seller in Varanasi suspects that his crushed camphor is mixed with sand. He heats a 50 g sample gently in a china dish under an inverted funnel with a cotton plug. After the heating, he scrapes 38 g of white solid from the inside of the funnel, and 11.5 g of sand is left in the dish.
(a) Why does the camphor collect on the funnel while the sand stays in the dish?
(b) Calculate the percentage by mass of sand in the sample.
(c) 38 g plus 11.5 g is less than 50 g. State the mass that is missing and one reason it could be missing.
(d) He must print either 76% camphor (what he collected) or 77% camphor (50 g minus the sand). Choose one and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Camphor sublimes on heating and deposits on the cooler funnel, while sand does not sublime. (b) 11.5/50 x 100 = 23%. (c) 50 - 38 - 11.5 = 0.5 g; some camphor vapour may not have deposited on the funnel and was lost. (d) A reasoned choice: 77% counts the 0.5 g as camphor, which is likely if the sand is weighed accurately, while 76% claims only what was actually collected and is the safer measured figure.
s: (a) Camphor sublimes, sand does not
(b) 23% sand
(c) 0.5 g missing with a plausible reason
(d) A justified choice between 76% and 77%

questions.q:
A student in Bharatpur runs 5 mL of mustard oil and 20 mL of water through a separating funnel. She collects 19 mL of clear water, then a 2 mL portion that is cloudy and holds 1 mL of oil and 1 mL of water, and finally 4 mL of oil.
(a) Which liquid drains first and why?
(b) How much of the oil was collected pure, as a percentage of the 5 mL, and what percentage of the water was collected pure?
(c) Why does the method set aside the mixed portion?
(d) She can discard the 2 mL portion or pour it into the next batch to separate again. Choose one and say what is gained or lost.
questions.a: (a) Water, because it is denser and forms the lower layer. (b) Oil: 4/5 x 100 = 80% pure; water: 19/20 x 100 = 95% pure. (c) The portion holds both liquids, so adding it to either would make that liquid impure. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. discarding keeps both products pure but wastes 1 mL of each liquid; adding it to the next batch recovers the liquids but needs another run to separate it again.
s: (a) Water first because it is denser
(b) 80% oil and 95% water
(c) The portion contains both liquids
(d) A justified choice naming the gain and the loss

questions.q: In Activity 5.1 a thin laser beam is passed through three beakers: salt stirred in water, chalk powder stirred in water, and a few drops of milk in water. In which beakers is the path of the beam visible from the side?
questions.a: The chalk and water beaker and the milk and water beaker, but not the salt and water beaker
o: The chalk and water beaker and the milk and water beaker, but not the salt and water beaker
The salt and water beaker only, because it is the clearest
All three beakers, because every liquid scatters light
The milk and water beaker only, because the chalk settles before the beam passes

questions.q: Three mixtures have particles of diameter 0.4 nm, 300 nm and 5000 nm. Which statement about them is correct?
questions.a: Only the 5000 nm mixture settles on standing, while the 300 nm mixture scatters light yet stays evenly dispersed
o: Only the 5000 nm mixture settles on standing, while the 300 nm mixture scatters light yet stays evenly dispersed
The 300 nm mixture settles on standing, because its particles are bigger than those of a solution
The 0.4 nm mixture scatters light, because its particles are the smallest

Three beakers are tested for a class. Beaker A holds salt dissolved in water (particles 0.5 nm), beaker B holds chalk powder in water (particles 3000 nm) and beaker C holds a few drops of milk in water (particles 200 nm). A laser beam is passed through each and the beakers are left undisturbed for ten minutes. In A the beam is invisible and nothing settles; in B the beam is visible and a white layer forms at the bottom; in C the beam is visible and nothing settles.
(a) Name the type of mixture in each beaker.
(b) Why does C look uniform and yet show the beam?
(c) Predict what each beaker looks like after a whole day.
(d) A fourth beaker D has particles of 800 nm and nothing settles in ten minutes. Decide whether D is a suspension or a colloid, and say whether the ten-minute wait alone proves it.
questions.a: (a) A is a solution, B a suspension and C a colloid. (b) Its particles, 1 to 1000 nm, stay evenly dispersed so it looks uniform, but they are big enough to scatter the light. (c) A and C unchanged; B with the chalk settled at the bottom. (d) D is a colloid, because 800 nm lies between 1 nm and 1000 nm; a suspension has particles above 1000 nm. The ten-minute wait alone does not prove it, since even a suspension's particles may need longer to settle, so the particle size or the full-day behaviour decides.
s: (a) Solution, suspension, colloid
(b) Colloid particles scatter light yet stay dispersed
(c) A and C unchanged, B settled
(d) D classified as colloid using 800 nm against 1000 nm

questions.q:
A panchayat in a hill village treats the muddy water of a 200 L storage tank using powdered alum. The notebook plan is 2 g of alum for every 10 L of water. In a trial the clumps settled completely after two hours, but after thirty minutes the water was still cloudy.
(a) Calculate the mass of alum the plan needs for the tank.
(b) Name what alum does to the fine particles.
(c) How should the settled clumps be removed?
(d) Only 30 g of alum is in stock. Find how many litres it can treat at the notebook plan, and decide whether to use all of it on the whole 200 L tank or treat only that volume.

(d) 30 g / 2 g x 10 L = 150 L. Treating only 150 L follows the plan; spreading 30 g over 200 L gives less than the planned dose, so some fine particles may stay unclumped and the water cloudy. Treat 150 L now.
s: (a) 40 g of alum
(b) Alum makes the fine particles clump together
(c) Decantation or filtration
(d) 150 L found and a justified choice
